BEWARE: There are minor spoilers for Magi within this post!

Magi: The Labyrinth of Magic can be most aptly described as an action shounen, yet this show manages to achieve much more than most of its peers.

Set in an Arabic-themed fantasy world (with references to The Arabian Nights, galore), Magi details the journey of a young magi named Aladdin. A magi is one of a select group of people who boast immense magical power due to a blessing by the Rukh (the life force/source of magic of the Magi universe). These magi are the one's who choose the kings of the world, and they do so by selecting a King's Candidate and having them complete a dungeon. This may all sound very run-of-the-mill and bland, but viewers are quickly introduced to Alibaba, a young man who is indentured to a wealthy noble. Alibaba is the main focus of the show. As we soon discover, he is Aladdin's King's Candidate. As cliched as it is, there is more to Alibaba than we first realize, and much of the show revolves around Alibaba, his past, and his future.

Action shounen are generally known for fight scenes, young and brash lead characters, and slightly immature tomfoolery. Magi has all of these things, but not in excess. This works to the show's benefit, unlike other shows that bombard the viewer with the same tropes, repeatedly. While Magi does succumb to these, it uses them sparingly, and in a way that doesn't get tiresome. However, what really sets Magi apart is that it reaches beyond its genre to give its viewers something more; something rare in the action shounen genre: A well-realized message.

Magi explores the nature of destiny, and how one's view of destiny affects their actions. As events unfold, viewers come across characters who believe that they can change their fate and move on to a better tomorrow, as well as characters who curse their fates and believe that the only thing they can do is destroy the system that placed such a yoke upon them. By the end of the show, a clear answer is not given (though an answer may be arrived at in the second season, which I have not viewed). The viewer is left wondering why poverty, war, and other manmade suffering exists. Do not all people simply wish to be happy? Likewise, is it wrong for people who see no other way out to try to tear off the bonds that are holding them in place? Or is it possible to work towards a new future without destroying others? Is it possible to walk a purely righteous path in the world? Or must people tread a path, both good and evil, to make the best possible world? These are the questions that Magi: The Labyrinth of Magic asks.

Many action shounen wax philosophical about the power of friendship and the value of guts, but Magi asks more nuanced questions. Such is what sets it apart from it's contemporaries. In addition to this, Magi has an interesting cast of characters, each of which has a distinct personality and set of motivations. Some characters fall into generic, anime archetypes, but end up upturning those tropes by acting in a complex fashion. There are also plenty of good action scenes and cool powers for people who enjoy a good, mindless shounen. However, if you'd like to analyze the message that Magi wants to send, the show invites you to do so. Magi is by no means a perfect anime, nor is it the best shounen. Many seinen titles convey their themes in a more intricate fashion than Magi, and other shounen, generally can. Even still Magi is a very good anime, and earned an 8/10 from me.

Prisoner's Dilemma.

If everyone agrees, it makes sense to deviate and spy since you'll have all the information. If one or more deviates, it makes sense to deviate yourself since that will put you on an even playing field. In all cases, it makes sense to deviate, and therefore while the results are likely better for everyone if they could just cooperate, their individual circumstances make it impossible.

I don't think the Prisoner's dilemma suggests that in all cases it makes sense to deviate/spy, but rather that because deviating/spying offers the best possible outcome, self-interest would naturally lead one to choose this option. That being said, it is certainly applicable in this case because it involves cooperative behavior.
